rewritten_text:
Biddy wept. Through my own tears the darkening garden, the lane, and the emerging stars all blurred together.

‘Nothing was ever found out, Biddy?’

‘Nothing.’

‘Do you know what has become of Orlick?’

‘Judging by the colour of his clothes, I imagine he works in the quarries.’

‘Then you must have seen him? Why are you looking at that dark tree in the lane?’

‘I saw him there the night she died.’

‘And that wasn’t the last time, was it, Biddy?’

‘No. I have seen him there while we’ve been walking here. It’s no use,’ she added, putting her hand on my arm as I started to run out. ‘You know I wouldn’t mislead you. He stayed less than a minute, and now he’s gone.’

Learning that this fellow still pursued her rekindled all my anger, and my hostility toward him hardened. I told her so, declaring that I would spend whatever money and take whatever trouble were needed to drive him out of the district. Gradually she guided our conversation toward calmer subjects. She told me how much Joe loved me, and how he never complained about anything. She did not say about me; there was no need, for I understood. He simply fulfilled the duties of his life with strong hands, few words, and a gentle heart.

‘Indeed, it would be difficult to praise him too much,’ I said. ‘And Biddy, we must talk of these things often, because naturally I shall come here frequently now. I will not leave poor Joe by himself.’

Biddy did not answer.

‘Biddy, can’t you hear me?’

‘Yes, Mr. Pip.’

‘Leaving aside your calling me Mr. Pip—which strikes me as rather inappropriate, Biddy—what do you mean?’

‘What do I mean?’ Biddy asked timidly.

‘Biddy,’ I said, asserting myself with an air of virtue, ‘I must insist that you explain what you mean by this.’

‘By this?’ said Biddy.

‘Now don’t repeat everything,’ I snapped. ‘You never used to repeat everything, Biddy.’

‘Used to!’ said Biddy. ‘Oh, Mr. Pip! Used to!’

Well, I thought I had better abandon that argument too. After another silent circuit of the garden, I returned to my principal point.

‘Biddy,’ I said, ‘I remarked that I would often come here to visit Joe, and you met that remark with a conspicuous silence. Please be good enough to explain why.’

‘Are you quite certain, then, that you WILL visit him often?’ Biddy asked. She stopped on the narrow garden path and looked at me beneath the stars with clear, honest eyes.

It was after two when a sudden turning brought me beside the lake, near a small inlet where a skiff lay moored. Our house was not far distant, and I caught sight of my father and aunt walking on the lawn. I sprang into the boat and, being well practised in such undertakings, pushed away from the bank and strained every muscle to row quickly across. My father has often told me that, as I approached in white, with only my tartan rachan over me, my hair flowing upon my shoulders, and the boat flying faster than he could have thought my strength capable of driving it, I resembled a spirit more than a mortal girl. I reached the shore; my father steadied the boat; I sprang lightly out, and the next instant found myself in his arms.

Now, indeed, my life began. The dull sameness of everything around me gave way to the most brilliant scene of pleasure and joy. My happiness in my father’s society surpassed even my eager expectations. We were constantly together, and our conversation could never be exhausted. During his sixteen years away he had lived among peoples scarcely known in Europe. He had travelled through Persia, Arabia, and northern India, entering the dwellings of their inhabitants with a liberty granted to few Europeans. When we wearied of discussing our plans for the future, his accounts of their customs, his anecdotes, and his pictures of the landscape filled hours of exquisite enjoyment.

Affection spoke in a voice so unfamiliar to me that I listened with rapture when he described his feelings for me through those long years of seeming neglect. ‘At first,’ he said, ‘I could not endure the thought of my poor little daughter. Afterwards, as sorrow lessened and hope returned, I could turn only to her. In cities and deserts alike, her small fairy figure, as I pictured it, was always passing before my eyes. The northern wind refreshed me with a greater sweetness and softness because it appeared to bear something of your spirit. Often I resolved to return at once and carry you away to a fruitful island, where we might live forever in peace. On my journey home, so many fears troubled my ardent hopes that impatience became an intolerable pain. I dared not imagine the sun shining and the moon rising upon your grave instead of your living figure. But no, that has not happened; I possess my Mathilda, my comfort and my hope.’

‘Stop the stabboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Stop the labboard! Ahead on the stabboard! Stop her! Turn your outside over easy! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Run out that head-line! Quick about it! Come along—out with the spring-line—what are you doing there? Take the bight round that stump! Ready by the stage—let her go! Finished with the engines, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!’—testing the gauge-cocks.

Tom kept whitewashing, taking no notice of the steamboat. Ben watched for a moment, then exclaimed, ‘Hi-yi! You’re in a fix, ain’t you!’

There was no reply. Tom inspected his latest stroke with an artist’s gaze, drew the brush gently over the fence again, and examined his achievement as before. Ben moved up beside him. The apple set Tom’s mouth watering, but he remained at his task. Ben said:

‘Hello, old fellow, they’ve got you working, have they?’

Tom spun round suddenly.

‘Why, Ben, it’s you! I didn’t notice.’

‘Say, I’m off swimming. Don’t you wish you could come? Of course, though, you’d sooner work, wouldn’t you? Sure you would!’

Tom considered his companion briefly and asked:

‘What do you mean by work?’

‘Why, isn’t that work?’

Returning to his whitewashing, Tom replied indifferently:

‘Maybe it is, maybe it ain’t. What I know is, Tom Sawyer’s satisfied with it.’

‘Oh, come along! You don’t pretend you actually like it?’

The brush never stopped.

‘Like it? Well, why shouldn’t I? Does a fellow have the chance to whitewash a fence every day?’

This gave the matter a different appearance. Ben ceased nibbling his apple. Tom moved his brush delicately to and fro, stepped back to judge the result, supplied a touch here and another there, and examined it afresh. Ben followed every motion, his interest and absorption increasing steadily. At last he said:

‘Say, Tom, let me do a little whitewashing.’

Tom reflected and seemed about to agree, but changed his mind.

‘No, no, Ben, I reckon that wouldn’t do. Aunt Polly’s mighty particular over this fence, you see, standing here on the street. If it was the back fence, neither she nor I would care. But she’s awful particular about this one. It needs the greatest care. I don’t suppose there’s one boy in a thousand—maybe two thousand—who can do it just right.’

‘Really? Is that true? Oh, come on, just let me try a little. I’d let you, Tom, if I was in your place.’

‘Ben, I’d like to, honest injun. But Aunt Polly—well, Jim asked to do it and she refused him; Sid asked too, and she wouldn’t even let Sid.’
